title: A-L-M
hook: olam, world, and ne'elam, hidden: Hasidic teachers say the world hides God

segments.voice: Yesterday, T-K-N: tikkun, setting right. Your line was fix. What crooked thing did you straighten? A new week of roots begins, and it starts with the word in tikkun olam. Day one thousand four hundred fifteen.

A small boy runs into his grandfather's study, crying. He'd been playing hide-and-seek. He found a good spot, hid, and waited. And waited. Finally he came out, and found that his friend had stopped looking long ago and wandered off. In the version people tell, the grandfather is a Hasidic rabbi, Rabbi Baruch of Medzhybizh, and when he hears it, he begins to cry too. God says the same thing, he tells the boy. I hide, and no one comes looking. Today's root holds the world and the hiding in the same letters.
screen: `A BOY HIDES, AND WAITS.` → `NOBODY IS LOOKING.` → `GOD SAYS THE SAME.`

segments.voice: A-L-M. Ayin, lamed, mem. Olam: world. And ne'elam: hidden. Turn it a few ways. First, time. In the Bible olam can reach toward time more than space: le-olam, forever. A psalm repeats it as a refrain, line after line: "for his mercy endureth for ever." Olam is a stretch so long you can't see its far end. Second, hidden. In Leviticus, a person touches something unclean, "and if it be hidden from him." The Hebrew is ne'lam, from these letters: something real that the person can't see. Third, Kohelet sets the word inside us: God "hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end." The word there is ha-olam, and readers have heard it as the world, or eternity, or something hidden: something vast placed in a person that they can't get to the end of. Fourth, the Hasidic teachers. They read the shared letters as a teaching: the world, olam, is the place where God is ne'elam, hidden. Creation is a kind of hiding place. Notice the difference between hidden and gone. Hidden means someone is there to be found. That's why the grandfather cried. A game of hide-and-seek only works if somebody goes looking.
screen: `OLAM: FOREVER.` · `NE'ELAM: HIDDEN FROM HIM.` · `THE WORLD SET IN THEIR HEART.` · `THE WORLD AS A HIDING PLACE.` · then, large: `HIDDEN IS NOT GONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for what's hidden. Settle, and breathe. Close your eyes and listen first, for the sounds under the obvious ones. A fridge humming, a bird, a car far off, your own breath. Then open your eyes and choose one ordinary object near you. Ask what's hidden in it: the hands that made it, the ground it came from, the road it took to reach you. Stay with that for a while. If you pray, the looking itself can be a kind of seeking. If you don't, let it simply be seeing. The bell holds the time.
screen: `LISTEN UNDER THE SOUNDS.` · `ONE ORDINARY OBJECT.` · `WHAT'S HIDDEN IN IT?`

segments.voice: A-L-M. Ayin, lamed, mem: olam, the world and forever, and ne'elam, hidden. A hiding place with someone in it. Today's word.
Your line: the world hides. Today, pick one thing you pass every day and look at it once as if something were tucked inside. Day one thousand four hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Hasidic teachers read olam, world, together with he'elem, hiddenness, and teach that the world both conceals God and invites seeking; a Hasidic story tells of a child whose friend stopped looking for him in hide-and-seek.

sources.ref: Hasidic teaching on olam and he'elem; the hide-and-seek story attributed to Rabbi Baruch of Medzhybizh

notes: Hide-and-seek story: commonly attributed to Rabbi Baruch of Medzhybizh and his grandson Yechiel (retold by Buber and others). Told here as 'the version people tell'. Confirm the attribution.
Olam/he'elem wordplay: a Hasidic teaching per the index; often cited in Chabad sources (e.g., Likkutei Torah) and elsewhere. No source named in the script. Confirm.
Psalm 136: 'ki le-olam chasdo' ends each verse; the script says 'a psalm repeats it as a refrain, line after line'. Confirm.
Ecclesiastes 3:11 ha-olam: readings as 'world', 'eternity' and 'hiddenness' are all attested among commentators; stated as 'readers have heard it as'. Confirm.
